title: Realization of a Superleak in a Quantum Gas
authors: Wan-Ling Yang, Shao-Bo Liu, Xiang Luo, Chao Yang, Hai-Lin Li, Yu-Zhou Yang, Yong-Kui Wang, Bing Yang
abstract: Ultracold quantum gases offer a controllable and microscopically accessible platform for understanding and engineering superfluidity. Yet, realizing a superleak that selectively transports the superfluid while suppressing normal flow has remained elusive. Here, we harness an optical superlattice to realize such a superleak through dynamical selectivity. The superfluid undergoes coherent Josephson transport, whereas the normal component exhibits slow, thermodynamically limited response, resulting in a flow-rate contrast of 500(49). Exploiting this contrast, we demonstrate repeated filtering of the normal component and dynamical purification of the superfluid, while sustaining coherent driven oscillations for up to 100 cycles. Our results establish a controllable atomic superleak and open possibilities for manipulating transport and thermodynamics in quantum fluids.
summary: The researchers engineered an optical superlattice to create a dynamical superleak in an ultracold quantum gas. By exploiting the vastly different transport rates between the superfluid and normal components, they developed a cyclic protocol to selectively filter out the normal component. This technique successfully purified the superfluid, allowing for the sustained observation of coherent Josephson oscillations over many cycles.
main_problem: The primary challenge addressed is realizing a superleak in a quantum gas that can selectively transport the superfluid component while strongly suppressing the normal flow.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated a controllable atomic superleak by exploiting the dynamical difference between coherent Josephson transport (superfluid) and slow, thermodynamically limited response (normal component). This allowed for the purification of the superfluid component and the maintenance of coherent oscillations for many cycles.
method: The superleak was realized dynamically using an optical superlattice potential and a cyclic protocol involving energy biasing and site-selective removal of atoms from the normal component.
model_or_system: The system uses ultracold quantum gases (e.g., Rb atoms) confined in a 3D optical dipole trap engineered with a bichromatic optical superlattice. The dynamics are modeled by distinguishing between coherent Josephson transport and incoherent, thermalization-limited normal transport.
key_observables: Flow-rate contrast (superfluid/normal ratio $\approx 500$), sustained coherent oscillations (up to 100 cycles), and the increasing condensate fraction (purification efficiency).
important_parameters: Tunneling energy ($J$), energy offset ($\Delta(t)$), and the characteristic timescales separating coherent (ms) and thermal (hundreds of ms) dynamics.
main_assumptions: The normal transport rate is assumed to scale with the thermalization rate ($\Gamma_{	ext{th}}$), and the superfluid dynamics are governed by Josephson coupling.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the conceptual superleak setup, the component separation in time-of-flight images, the site-selective removal protocol, and the sustained coherent oscillations achieved through purification cycles.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the physical problem (superleak realization) to detailing the mechanism (dynamical selectivity via optical superlattice), demonstrating the quantitative contrast, and finally presenting the purification protocol that sustains coherent dynamics.
why_interesting: This work provides an experimental realization of a quantum filter, which is highly relevant for understanding non-equilibrium quantum dynamics, quantum thermalization, and the manipulation of quantum coherence in many-body systems.
